query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a portion of the heavy elements (Hf, Mo, Ta) in as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with lighter elements (e.g., Al, Si) while maintaining the refractory elements (Ti, Zr) will reduce the density of the alloy without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: substitution of heavy elements with lighter ones (e.g., Al, Si) while maintaining refractory elements (Ti, Zr)
generation.conditions: room temperature to 1000 °C, unspecified loading conditions
generation.structural_mediator: solid solution formation with BCC structure
generation.mechanism: alloying and density reduction through substitution of heavy elements with lighter ones, maintaining refractory elements for high-temperature strength
generation.predicted_outcome: reduction in density by 5-10% relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr (from 10.21 g cm−3 to approximately 9.19-9.71 g cm−3), with maintained or improved mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures
generation.baseline: as-cast HfMoTaTiZr with a density of 10.21 g cm−3
generation.boundary: applicable up to 1000 °C, with unspecified loading conditions
generation.uncertainty: the exact amount of substitution required to achieve the desired density reduction without sacrificing mechanical properties is uncertain and requires further experimentation

falsification_experiment.design: prepare alloy samples with varying levels of substitution (e.g., 0%, 10%, 20%, 30% substitution of heavy elements with lighter ones), test their mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 1000 °C) using standardized testing protocols (e.g., tensile testing, compression testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the density of the alloy is reduced by more than 10% without maintaining or improving its mechanical properties at room temperature and elevated temperatures, the hypothesis is falsified (e.g., if the yield strength at room temperature or 1000 °C decreases by more than 10% relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr)

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [,,,,,]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. In this study, Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW RHEAs were designed for extremely high elevated-temperature strength by using the above guidelines: Ti and Zr of HfMoNbTaTiZr were replaced by W to increase the melting point and Young’s modulus. The proposed alloys will be compared with standard MoNbTaVW that contains vanadium instead of hafnium. Moreover, homogenization treatments at a temperature of 2100°C for 2 h, followed by air cooling, were conducted in an ultrahigh-temperature furnace in order to get the fully homogeneous state. Their microstructures and mechanical properties were investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and hardness and compression testing. The phase, temperature-dependent strength, and the ultrahigh elevated-temperature strength are discussed with the solution-strengthening mechanism, especially focusing on the contribution of edge-dislocation-induced strength.
